issues.legal_issue: The enactment of a special eviction procedure does not impliedly remove the government’s right to seek eviction under the ordinary law when the two remedies can coexist without contradiction or absurdity.
material_facts: The government leased public premises to the occupants for a fixed term, and the lease expired.
The government called on the occupants to return the premises and initiated proceedings under a special statute providing a speedier eviction procedure.
The statute did not expressly bar an ordinary suit, and its stated purpose was to add a speedier remedy to the existing one.
issues.conclusion: The special statute did not impliedly repeal or take away the government’s right to sue for eviction under the ordinary law.
issues.legal_principle: Implied repeal is disfavoured and is justified only where the later enactment is incompatible with the earlier law, makes their coexistence absurd or inconvenient, or otherwise necessarily displaces the earlier law. The Court relied on Re Drummond, [1891] 1 Ch. 524; Re Chance, [1936] Ch. 266; and the statement in The India, as quoted in Craies on Statute Law, 6th ed., p. 371. The later enactment’s affirmative provision of a speedier remedy did not exclude the ordinary suit remedy.

predicates.challenge_to_eviction_law: A party challenging an eviction law argues that its enactment removed an existing ordinary-law remedy.
predicates.later_law_adds_a_remedy: The later law provides an additional procedure for obtaining eviction rather than expressly excluding the prior procedure.
predicates.remedies_can_coexist_without_absurdity: The ordinary and special procedures can operate together without contradiction, inconvenience, or absurd consequences.

issues.definition: When an eviction-law challenge concerns a later law that adds a procedure and can coexist with the ordinary remedy without absurdity, the government retains the ordinary eviction suit remedy.

issues.legal_issue: Classifying occupants of publicly owned premises separately from occupants of privately owned premises is valid when the classification bears a rational relationship to the public interest in speedy recovery of public property.
material_facts: The challenged law applied a special procedure to occupants of public premises, distinguishing them from occupants of private premises.
The law’s object was to keep public premises free from encroachment and unauthorised occupation and to enable their speedy recovery.
The public has a vital interest in the recovery of public premises.
issues.conclusion: The classification between occupants of public premises and occupants of private premises was based on an intelligible differentia with a rational relationship to the law’s object and did not violate the equality guarantee.
issues.legal_principle: A classification is valid if it rests on an intelligible differentia distinguishing the grouped persons from others and that differentia has a rational relationship to the legislation’s object. Applying that test, the Court relied on Baburao Shantaram More v. The Bombay Housing Board, [1954] S.C.R. 572, which upheld differential treatment of tenants of public property where the classification was reasonably related to the legislative object.

predicates.challenge_to_public_property_classificat: A party challenges a law that treats occupants of public premises differently from occupants of private premises.
predicates.occupants_of_public_and_private_premises: The law places occupants of publicly owned premises in a distinct group from occupants of privately owned premises.
predicates.public_has_a_vital_interest_in_recovery: Members of the public have a vital interest in seeing the publicly owned premises freed from encroachment or unauthorised occupation.
predicates.speedy_recovery_is_the_legislative_objec: The law is intended to enable the prompt recovery of public premises.

issues.definition: If a challenged law separates occupants of public and private premises to advance speedy recovery in which the public has a vital interest, the classification is valid.

issues.legal_issue: Providing the government with a choice between an ordinary eviction suit and a more prejudicial summary procedure, without guiding the official’s choice, discriminates among similarly situated occupants of public premises.
material_facts: The government could seek eviction either by an ordinary suit or through the special procedure.

The special procedure was more prejudicial because an executive officer could order eviction on the basis of his satisfaction, with an appeal to another executive officer, rather than through an ordinary court proceeding.
The statute left the Collector’s choice of procedure unguided, allowing the more prejudicial procedure to be used against some occupants but not others who were similarly situated.
issues.conclusion: The special procedure was invalid because it conferred unguided discretion to select a more prejudicial remedy against some similarly situated occupants; the Court held that the provision authorising that procedure violated the equality guarantee.
issues.legal_principle: Equality protections apply to procedural laws as well as substantive laws. Where two procedures are available for similarly situated persons, and one is more drastic or prejudicial, allowing an authority to choose arbitrarily between them results in discrimination. The Court relied on State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali, [1952] S.C.R. 284; Suraj Mall Mohta v. A. V. Visvanatha Sastri, [1955] 1 S.C.R. 448; Shree Meenakshi Mills Ltd. v. A. V. Visvanathan Sastri, [1955] 1 S.C.R. 787; and Banarsi Das v. Cane Commissioner, U.P., [1963] Supp. 2 S.C.R. 760. It held the provision conferring the unguided choice void.

rule.if: challenge_to_public_premises_eviction_procedure and occupants_are_similarly_situated and ordinary_and_summary_remedies_are_both_available and summary_remedy_is_more_prejudicial and authority_has_unguided_choice

predicates.challenge_to_public_premises_eviction_pr: A party challenges a special procedure for evicting occupants of public premises.
predicates.occupants_are_similarly_situated: The persons subject to the alternative procedures belong to the same relevant class of occupants.
predicates.ordinary_and_summary_remedies_are_both_a: The government can pursue eviction either through an ordinary court action or through a separate summary procedure.
predicates.summary_remedy_is_more_prejudicial: The summary procedure is more adverse to an occupant than the ordinary court action.
predicates.authority_has_unguided_choice: The law leaves the choice between the procedures to an authority without guiding principles for making that choice.

issues.definition: When similarly situated occupants may face either of two available remedies, and an authority has unguided discretion to select the more prejudicial one, that unguided choice is invalid.
